## A Thursday afternoon with the tea trolley

The bourbon biscuits always go first. That is one of the things I have learnt since I started volunteering at Wensum Vale Hospice in March 2022. We now hide a packet for the late group, which may not sound entirely fair, but otherwise they wouldn’t get a look-in.

I do the Thursday tea trolley in the day therapy unit. There are four of us on a rota meant for six, after one volunteer moved to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren and another went off for a knee operation over the summer. We could do with two more people.

Before you decide it isn’t for you, I should say that I spent 41 years in bookkeeping, mostly for a builders’ merchant in Dereham. I had no nursing skills when I arrived and have acquired none since. Keeping ledgers straight does, however, turn out to be useful practice for remembering who takes what in their tea.

Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars. He also tells me about the 1953 floods most weeks, slightly differently each time. I have stopped correcting the dates. I am there to listen, not audit him.

My first week was not a demonstration of quiet competence. I spilled an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much she needed a tissue, then told me it was the best afternoon she’d had in a month. It was a reassuring start, once I had found something to mop up with.

I think people sometimes hear “hospice” and imagine that volunteering must be harrowing, or that you need special qualifications. On a Thursday, we usually see about 14 to 18 patients. Many come for the art group, a hand massage or simply some company. Most go home afterwards. The day unit is often noisy and rather jolly, with plenty of conversation going on around the trolley.

That isn’t to say every afternoon is easy. Some weeks are hard, and sad days do happen. The staff look after us when they do. I wouldn’t want to pretend otherwise, but nor would I want that to put someone off before they had seen what an ordinary Thursday is like.

What you need is to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. You don’t need to know the right thing to say about everything. I certainly don’t.

The commitment is **one Thursday a fortnight, from 1.30 to 4pm**. Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, does the induction, which takes about two hours. There is also a short online food hygiene course, paid for by the hospice. You aren’t expected to turn up knowing how everything works.

When I retired, I rather drifted for eighteen months. After so long at work, I found I had no regular reason to go out most weeks. Thursdays fixed that. I like having somewhere I am expected, people to catch up with and a useful job to do. I also like knowing where the spare bourbons are.

If you think you might join us, there is a **volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits, and no obligation. You can also ring Bridget on the volunteering line.

We need two more for the rota. It would be lovely if at least two people reading this came along to find out more. You needn’t decide anything beforehand. Come and have a cup of tea with us.
